entries.title: Pointers and arrays
entries.summary: Addresses, dereferencing, pointer arithmetic, how arrays relate to pointers.
entries.description: `&x` is the address of `x`; `*p` is the object `p` points to; `NULL` points to nothing and must not be dereferenced. Arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type: `p + 1` is `sizeof(*p)` bytes further. An array name converts to a pointer to its first element in most expressions, but it is not a variable: you cannot assign to it, and `sizeof` still sees the whole array. `void *` is a generic pointer that needs a cast (or an assignment in C) before use.

details.name: Uninitialised pointers
details.text: A pointer declared without a value points nowhere valid. Initialise it with `NULL` or an address.

mistakes: Dereferencing NULL or an uninitialised pointer.
Using a pointer after the object it pointed to ended (dangling pointer).

entries.title: malloc, calloc, realloc, free
entries.summary: Allocate, resize and release heap memory.
entries.description: `malloc` returns `size` uninitialised bytes; `calloc` returns `n*size` bytes set to zero; `realloc` changes the size of a block (it may move it, copying the content; on failure it returns NULL and the old block is still valid); `free` releases a block. All allocators return NULL on failure. Every block you allocate must be freed exactly once.

details.name: Safe realloc
details.text: `tmp = realloc(p, n); if (tmp == NULL) { …handle…; } else p = tmp;` — writing `p = realloc(p, n)` leaks the old block when it fails.

details.name: Casting
details.text: In C the cast of the result is optional (`int *p = malloc(n * sizeof *p);`).

mistakes: Forgetting the `+ 1` for the terminator when allocating a string.
Double free, use after free, and leaks (use `valgrind ./prog` to find them).

entries.title: struct, typedef, enum
entries.summary: Records, new type names and named constants.
entries.description: Members are accessed with `.` on a struct and `->` on a pointer to a struct (`p->x` ≡ `(*p).x`). Assigning a struct copies all its members, and a struct can be passed to and returned from functions by value. `typedef` gives a type another name; an `enum` gives names to small integer constants (the first is 0 unless set; the following increase by 1).
mistakes: Comparing two structs with `==` (not allowed): compare member by member.

entries.title: C strings
entries.summary: A string is a char array ended by '\0'.
entries.syntax:
char s[] = "Hola";   /* 5 bytes: H o l a \0 */
char *t = "Hola";    /* points to a read-only literal */
entries.description: There is no string type. A string is a sequence of chars ending with a zero byte, so a string of length n needs n + 1 bytes. A literal like `"Hola"` lives in read-only memory: do not modify it through a `char *`; use an array (`char s[] = "…"`) for a modifiable copy. Compare contents with `strcmp`, never with `==` (that compares addresses).

entries.title: string.h functions
entries.summary: Length, copy, concatenate, compare, search, duplicate and split.
entries.description: `strlen` does not count the terminator. `strcpy`/`strcat` do not check the destination size: it must be big enough. `strncpy` does not add a terminator if the source is `n` or more chars long. `strcmp` returns 0 when equal, negative if `a` < `b`, positive if `a` > `b`. `strchr` returns a pointer to the first match or NULL. `strdup` returns a `malloc`ed copy you must `free`. `strtok` splits in place (it writes `\0` into the string, so use a copy) and remembers its position in hidden state; `strtok_r` is the re-entrant version.

details.name: memcpy / memset
details.text: Work on raw bytes with an explicit length: `memcpy(dst, src, n)`, `memset(p, 0, n)`.

mistakes: Using `strcmp(a, b)` as if it returned 1 for equal.
Passing a string literal to `strtok` (it must be modifiable).
